subject: Medicine
summary: Aortic dissection is a tear in the aortic intima allowing blood to split the media, creating a true and false lumen. Rapid diagnosis and appropriate tiered treatment are critical to prevent death.

sections.p: A tear in the aortic intima lets blood enter the media, forming a false lumen. Diagnosis relies on imaging that shows the intimal flap and lumen separation.
b: CT angiography is the gold‑standard; shows flap, true/false lumen, and extent.
Trans‑esophageal echo is useful when CT unavailable or patient unstable.

t.b: Does the aorta have an intimal flap? → Positive confirms dissection; location defines type.
Can we visualize a flap in the proximal aorta? → Positive supports diagnosis when CT not feasible.
Is there a widened mediastinum? → Suggestive but not definitive; normal does not rule out dissection.

sections.p: The Stanford classification guides therapy: Type A involves the ascending aorta; Type B is confined to the descending aorta.
b: Type A → surgical emergency.
Type B → medical management unless complications arise.

sections.p: Most dissections arise from chronic hypertension damaging the media; connective‑tissue disorders and other conditions increase risk.
b: Uncontrolled hypertension (most common).
Marfan syndrome or other connective‑tissue disease.
Bicuspid aortic valve.
Syphilitic aortitis (more common in low‑resource settings).
Trauma, iatrogenic injury, cocaine use.

sections.p: Patients describe sudden, severe tearing or ripping chest or back pain, often with radiation to the back, neck, or abdomen. Physical clues may include pulse or blood‑pressure differences between limbs.
b: Pain onset is abrupt, unlike crescendo angina.
Unequal arm blood pressures or absent femoral pulses.
New aortic regurgitation murmur in Type A.

sections.p: Imaging confirms the diagnosis; bedside tests help when imaging is delayed.
b: Rapid bedside ultrasound can detect pericardial effusion in proximal dissections.

t.a: Blood pressure measurement in both arms
t.b: Is there a >20 mmHg difference? → Suggests involvement of the arch (Type A).
Is it markedly elevated? → High sensitivity rule‑out test; normal does not exclude dissection.

sections.p: Complications can be rapidly fatal; early recognition saves lives.
b: Cardiac tamponade from rupture into pericardium (Type A).
Acute aortic regurgitation.
Organ malperfusion – stroke, renal failure, limb ischemia.
Rupture into pleural cavity.

sections.p: Control blood pressure and shear stress, then definitive therapy based on type.
b: IV β‑blocker (e.g., esmolol) first to reduce heart rate <60 bpm.
Add vasodilator (e.g., nitroprusside) only after β‑blockade to lower systolic <120 mmHg.
Type A → emergent surgical repair of ascending aorta.
Type B → intensive‑care medical therapy; endovascular stent if complications.

sections.p: Long‑term control of blood pressure and surveillance imaging reduce recurrence.
b: Target BP <130/80 mmHg with oral β‑blocker or ARB.
Serial CT or MRI at 3, 6, and 12 months, then annually.
Counsel on avoiding heavy lifting and illicit stimulants.

sections.p: Several acute chest conditions mimic dissection.
b: Acute myocardial infarction – crushing chest pain, ST changes.
Pulmonary embolism – pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia.
Pericarditis – sharp pain relieved by leaning forward.
Aortic aneurysm rupture – similar pain but often hypotensive without flap.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal chest X‑ray does not exclude dissection.
D‑dimer can be normal in early or limited dissections.
ECG may be normal or show nonspecific changes.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden tearing chest or back pain with unequal arm blood pressures
Loss of pulse or cold limb

faq.q: Why is blood pressure control more important than pain control?
faq.a: Shear stress from high pressure drives the tear; lowering pressure stops propagation, while pain relief alone does not.

faq.q: Can a dissection heal without surgery?
faq.a: Type B dissections often stabilize with medical therapy; Type A usually requires surgery to prevent rupture.

faq.q: What is the role of D‑dimer?
faq.a: A high D‑dimer supports the diagnosis, but a normal result cannot rule out a dissection.

exam: Explain the Stanford classification and its therapeutic implications.
List the first‑line pharmacologic steps in acute aortic dissection and why β‑blockade precedes vasodilation.
Describe three red‑flag complications that mandate immediate intervention.
